issues.legal_issue: A plaintiff whose title has already been finally adjudicated must seek a separate declaration of title before bringing a suit to recover possession.
material_facts: The owners’ title to the property was upheld in earlier writ proceedings, and that finding was not overturned.
The claimant participated in the appeal in which the title finding was made.
The earlier court left the dispute over recovery of possession from the occupants open.
The owners later brought a suit seeking possession.
issues.conclusion: The earlier title determination operated as res judicata, so the owners could sue for possession on the basis of that title without seeking a separate declaration.
issues.legal_principle: A final adjudication of title binding on a party operates as res judicata; where title has already been adjudicated, a suit to recover possession on that title does not require a further declaration of title.

predicates.possession_recovery_suit: The plaintiff brings a proceeding seeking recovery of possession of property.
predicates.title_previously_adjudicated: A court has already finally determined the plaintiff’s title to the property.
predicates.claimant_bound_by_prior_title_decision: The opposing claimant was bound by the earlier title determination.

issues.definition: When a possession-recovery suit follows a binding prior determination of the plaintiff’s title, a separate title declaration is not required.

issues.legal_issue: In a suit to recover possession based on established title, the defendant bears the burden of proving that adverse possession has displaced that title.
material_facts: The owners’ title had been finally adjudicated in earlier proceedings.
The owners brought a suit to recover possession on the basis of that title.
The claimant argued that the suit was governed by the limitation rule for possession based on prior possession and asserted adverse possession.
issues.conclusion: The suit attracted Article 65 of the Schedule to the Limitation Act, 1963, and the claimant had to prove possession under a hostile title sufficient to extinguish the owners’ title.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 65 of the Limitation Act, 1963, limitation begins when the defendant’s possession becomes adverse. Once the plaintiff proves title, the burden shifts to the defendant to establish title by adverse possession; the Court relied on M. Durai v. Muthu & Ors. and Saroop Singh v. Banto & Ors.

predicates.possession_recovery_suit: The plaintiff brings a proceeding seeking recovery of possession of property.
predicates.plaintiff_title_proved: The plaintiff establishes title to the property.
predicates.defendant_relies_on_adverse_possession: The defendant asserts that possession has extinguished the plaintiff’s title by adverse possession.

issues.definition: When a plaintiff establishes title in a possession-recovery suit and the defendant relies on adverse possession, the defendant must prove adverse possession.

issues.legal_issue: Long possession does not establish title by adverse possession unless it is hostile to the true owner and continues with the necessary character for the limitation period.
material_facts: The claimant and her husband claimed the land under an allotment from the Slum Clearance Board and had paid instalments under that arrangement.
The claimant did not assert an independent claim by adverse possession before the writ appeal and did not claim adverse title from the commencement of possession.
The claimant relied on long possession, but the Board had no title to transfer the property.
The claimant did not establish the required hostile possession against the owners for the limitation period.
issues.conclusion: The claimant had not acquired title by adverse possession; long possession and a claim derived from the Board did not establish the required hostile intent.
issues.legal_principle: Adverse possession requires possession adverse to the true owner, with animus possidendi existing from the commencement of possession and continuing for the prescribed period. Possession must be open, hostile, continuous, and adequate in continuity, publicity, and extent; mere long possession is insufficient. The Court relied on Saroop Singh v. Banto & Ors., T. Anjanappa & Ors. v. Somalingappa & Anr., and P.T. Munichikkanna Reddy & Ors. v. Revamma & Ors.

rule.if: possession_recovery_suit and adverse_possession_claim and (not hostile_intent_at_possession_start or not open_continuous_hostile_possession)

predicates.possession_recovery_suit: The plaintiff brings a proceeding seeking recovery of possession of property.
predicates.adverse_possession_claim: The defendant claims to have acquired title through adverse possession.
predicates.hostile_intent_at_possession_start: The defendant’s possession was hostile to the true owner from its commencement.
predicates.open_continuous_hostile_possession: The defendant possessed the property openly, continuously, and in a manner hostile to the true owner for the required period.

issues.definition: In a possession-recovery suit, a claim of adverse possession does not acquire title if possession lacked hostile intent from its commencement or was not open, continuous, and hostile.
